Thank you, Your Excellency, Vice President of the Human Rights Council. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, fellow mandate holders, colleagues, it is a pleasure to address the Human Rights Council in my capacity as chair of the UN Working Group of Experts on People of African Descent.

Today, I will.

Present our activities over the past year, including the findings, conclusions, and recommendations of our 2026 thematic report on racialization and global migration, and the reports of our visits to Suriname and Mexico. Since our last report to the Council, we held our 37th and 38th sessions in Geneva. Our discussions covered migration and human mobility, the 25th anniversary of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, and recent developments in the global reparatory justice agenda. We also held an expert consultation on the land rights of people of African descent, which will be the thematic focus of our 39th session in November 2026. The working group remained actively engaged with member states, United Nations human rights mechanisms, civil society, and other stakeholders, with particular attention to promoting the implementation of the second International Decade for People of African Descent and strengthening cooperation with the other United Nations anti-racism mechanisms. Excellencies, our thematic report, Crossings and Journeys, People of African Descent in Global Migration and the Enduring Architecture of Racialization, is the result of extensive consultations during our 37th session. I thank the experts, member states, civil society, and other participants for their written contributions and valuable insights. These contributions highlighted that human mobility is not experienced equally. For Africans and people of African descent, the freedom to move continues to be shaped by racial hierarchies with deep historical roots. This legacy continues today as some people are welcomed as expatriates, while others are treated simply as migrants. Some are seen as part of the circulation of talent, while others are presented as a crisis to be managed. The working group found that precarity in migration is not accidental, but the result of policy choices. The loss of life and liberty among Africans and people of African descent on the move remains a serious concern. Racism deepens their vulnerability. It increases the risk of trafficking, racial profiling, denial of protection, deportation, sexual and gender-based violence, exploitation, and abuse. Technology is also creating new challenges. Artificial intelligence, biometric systems, and digital surveillance are increasingly used to control migration. Instead of reducing inequality, these technologies can reinforce racial discrimination. Deportation can also cause serious harm. It is often preceded by detention and can lead to the loss of possessions, wages, and dignity. It can separate families, disrupt lives, and cause lasting trauma. The working group concluded that deportation should not be the default response to irregular migration. In this context, regularization should not be seen as an exception or a privilege. It is an important way to correct systems that themselves produce irregularity. It should be based on dignity, security, legal certainty, and full participation in society. The working group stresses the need for a more humane approach to migration. To humanize migration is to confront the violence that shapes perceptions of mobility and determines whose suffering counts and whose does not. The working group made several recommendations, including the following. Member states should ensure that migration and border policies are based on human rights, dignity, and racial justice. They should prevent racial profiling and expand safe and regular migration pathways for Africans and people of African descent. The working group also calls on states to recognize that the legacies of enslavement and colonialism continue to shape the experiences of African and Afro-descendant migrants. Migration should therefore be included in discussions and actions on reparatory justice. Migration policies should move away from criminalization and exclusion and instead focus on healing. States should ensure that migrants can access health care, education, labor protection, and justice without fear of arrest or deportation. Special attention should be given to women and girls who are more at risk of abuse along migration routes. Finally, the Working Group recommends stronger safeguards for the use of artificial intelligence and other technologies at borders. These systems must respect international human rights standards and be used with transparency, monitoring, and accountability. I now turn to the Working Group's visit to Suriname at the invitation of the government. During the visit, we met with government officials, national institutions, civil society organizations, and Afro-descendant and indigenous communities. The working group thanks the government of Suriname for its cooperation and all the communities and organizations that shared experiences and testimonies with us. We identified several positive developments and welcome efforts to advance reparatory justice and establish an independent national human rights institution. However, serious concerns came up during the visit. Land rights remain one of the biggest challenges. The collective rights of Maroon communities over the lands and resources still lack legal recognition. The implementation of judgments of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights remains slow, while mining and logging activities continue on traditional territories without adequate consultation and consent. Gold mining has also contributed to deforestation, river pollution, and severe mercury contamination. The working group saw significant inequalities affecting people of African descent across the country, particularly in the interior, where access to adequate housing, employment, healthcare, and other essential services remains difficult. We were especially concerned about the situation of children, including the high rates of early pregnancy among girls as young as 12 or 13. Children of African descent also face racial discrimination in access to education. The working group heard that some Rastafari students were denied access to schools simply because they wear their hair in locks. Significant gaps in disaggregated data make it difficult to develop effective policies. In the criminal justice system, we heard about the overrepresentation of Afro-Surinamese men and boys in detention. They also reportedly face more severe penalties than others. We received reports of reprisals against activists, including incarceration for defending their collective rights. Based on these findings, the working group made several recommendations, of which I will highlight a few. The working group calls on Suriname to move from commitment to action. This includes accelerating progress on the collective rights of Maroon communities and guaranteeing free, prior, and informed consent in decisions affecting their lands. We also recommend comprehensive legislation against racial discrimination, including stronger protection against racial profiling and racist hate speech. Access to health care, adequate housing, and employment should be improved, particularly in the interior. In education, we recommend stronger measures to prevent discrimination against children of African descent, as well as including the history of slavery, colonialism, and the contributions of people of African descent in school curricula. Finally, greater protection and support are needed to women and girls against sexual and gender-based violence. We also call for measures to address the high rates of early pregnancy, including comprehensive sexual education and access to family planning. The working group encourages Suriname to implement these recommendations in close cooperation with people of African descent and the communities concerned, and we stand ready to support these efforts. I will now turn to the working group's visit to Mexico. For colleagues in interpretation, I will now continue in Spanish. During the visit, we were in Mexico City and in the states of Veracruz, Guerrero, and Oaxaca, where we met with representatives from government, civil society organizations, and Afro-Mexican communities. Agadecemos al gobierno de Mexico su cooperacion, asi como a todas las personas, comunidades y organizaciones que compartieron con nosotras sus experiencias y testimonios. El grupo de trabajo reconoce los importantes progresos realizados por Mexico, en particular el reconocimiento constitucional de los pueblos y comunidades afromexicanas en 2019, reforzado por la reforma constitucional de 2024. así como la mejora de su visibilidad estadística y los actuales esfuerzos por avanzar en políticas de igualdad y no discriminación. También tomamos nota de diversas iniciativas impulsadas por las autoridades para fortalecer la inclusión, la participación y el acceso a servicios de las comunidades afromexicanas. However, important challenges persist for this recognition to be fully translated into the enjoyment of human rights. There are also gaps in the data on political participation, migration and asylum, access to justice, disappearances and deprivation of liberty. The profile racial sigue siendo otro grave problema vinculado a la persistente asociación entre negritud y extranjería. Recibimos testimonios sobre detenciones y controles migratorios basados en la apariencia física y el color de piel, incluyendo casos de personas afromexicanas a quienes se les había pedido cantar el himno nacional para demostrar que eran mexicanas. The group of work also received information about water contamination that could be related to serious health problems and deaths, as well as about insufficient responses to natural disasters. In Cordoba, families of Afro-descendants linked to the Patio de la Estrella face alleged cases of harassment, institutional persecution, and risk of eviction in a context of gentrification. Las mujeres y niñas afrodescendientes enfrentan además formas interrelacionadas de discriminación racial y de género. Nos preocupa especialmente la violencia obstétrica. Algunas mujeres explicaron que el estereotipo de que las mujeres negras pueden soportar más el dolor puede traducirse en retrasos y un trato discriminatorio durante el embarazo y el parto. También recibimos información sobre la creciente violencia contra las personas LGBTIQ+, incluidos asesinatos de defensores de derechos humanos, así como sobre la persistencia de la impunidad y las limitaciones en las investigaciones. I want to remember Sael Silva Cisneros, lawyer, activist, Afro-Mexican and human rights defender, with whom we met during our visit and who was assassinated weeks later in Guerrero. The working group condemned his murder and demanded a prompt, exhaustive and impartial investigation to clarify the facts and determine responsibilities. I didn't want to conclude this presentation without remembering it. On the basis of these findings, the working group formulated several recommendations, and I would like to highlight some. Mexico must ensure that the constitutional recognition of Afro-Mexican peoples is accompanied by legitimate representation, effective participation, and data that makes discrimination visible. Mexico debe prevenir y combatir el perfilamiento racial y asegurar que las personas afrodescendientes puedan acceder a la justicia sin discriminación. También se debe garantizar el acceso a la educación, la salud, la vivienda, el agua y otros servicios esenciales en condiciones de igualdad. Esto incluye prevenir el acoso racista en las escuelas y el trato discriminatorio en los servicios de salud. Mexico debe proteger los derechos territoriales y ambientales de las comunidades afrodescendientes, garantizar su participación efectiva en las decisiones que les afectan y protegerlas frente a los desalojos forzosos, el desplazamiento y la gentrificación. The group of trabajo recomienda avanzar en una estrategia nacional de memoria, verdad y reparación que reconozca los legados de la esclavitud y del racismo anti negro y apoye iniciativas como el propuesto Museo Nacional de los Pueblos Afrodescendientes. El grupo de trabajo está dispuesto a seguir colaborando con el gobierno de México para apoyar la aplicación de estas recomendaciones. Señora vicepresidenta, con esto concluyo mi presentación, esperando escuchar ahora las delegaciones. Gracias.
